name: Bruise
lede: Bruise is the color of a bruise: a dull, reddish purple that is named for the injury, not for any dye or pigment.

sections.title: Named for an injury
sections.body:
The word names the injury, and the color it names is a muted purple that sits between [[plum]] and [[eggplant]] [1]. Our library finds it in the color lists of Ridgway (1912), Maerz and Paul (1930), ISCC-NBS (1955) and the xkcd survey (2010), and its nearest named color is Plum, 4.7 units away [1]. Two near-duplicates, Secret and Pansy Violet, appear in the same lists [1].

The swatch is a still image, but the books use the bruise for a color in motion.

sections.title: Colors that change like a bruise
sections.body:
Two writers use the bruise as a picture of a dye in the act of developing. Finlay describes a purple dye, painted onto cloth, as a stain that is lime green, then yellow, then purple, like a bruise [2]. The effect comes from a light-sensitive compound in the dye, which turns purple on exposure to sunshine and otherwise stays green [2]. Finlay adds that this is strictly painting, not dyeing, and that if anyone had found a way to fix the compound it could have made the world's first photographs [2].

In a second book Finlay recalls pulling dye from sea snails onto cotton thread with a Mexican guide, and watching the yarn change color like a bruise: yellow, then green, then lavender [3]. Compare [[tyrian-purple]], the purple of the ancient dye trade. The bruise comparison is a modern writer's image, not an ancient name for the color [2][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Bruise is almost absent from our paintings archive: one painting out of 23,781 holds it, a work dated 1900, and the color is rarer there than 86% of the named colors, as photographed [1].

The word peaks in the 2010s and rose fastest in the 1950s, in adjective use only [1]. The match is a look-alike hue in a photograph of a varnished painting, not evidence of a bruise-colored pigment.
